In his State of the Union, President Bush declared plans to "double the current capacity of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve," (SPR) a move that would involve increasing government reserves to 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil. The timeline for completion of this "ramp-up" is by 2027.

text:
The plan to increase the SPR to 1.5 billion barrels of crude by 2027 is set to start with the government purchasing 100,000 barrels per day beginning in the spring of 2007. After a few months of such purchases the government would re- assess its performance and the present crude price situation. The government would then evaluate when and where to buy the remaining crude needed to fill the SPR to the announced capacity. Filling the SPR to 1.5 billion barrels of crude would involve a net increase of more than 800 million barrels over the 20-year window the government has set out. This increase is therefore equivalent to approximately 110,000 barrels of oil per day through 2027. Though such an increase would represent just a fraction of the 5 million barrels of oil that the US produces domestically every day, as well as of the more than 10 million barrels of oil that the US imports every day, this increase is nonetheless quite significant.
Some sources indicate that the desired source for this SPR crude will be increased domestic capacity. Even if domestic sources do supply this additional crude, the tapering production of mature domestic fields and increasing demand levels should force import levels to increase by at least 110,000 barrels per day in order to fill the SPR to its desired level. Over the last 12 months, the largest sources of crude imports have been Canada, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, Venezuela, and Nigeria. Firm Orders (133) Another sign that the crewing issue is being addressed is an announcement by Japanese ship owner NYK and Korea's Hyundai Heavy Industries that they plan to build an LNG training vessel. This ship will be able to offer onboard training to 20 trainees at a time. A yard in China is also building similar facilities on one of its new builds in order to train local cadets. Meanwhile, Russia's Sovcomflot has acquired two ships from BG which it will utilize to train crews in preparation for operating tonnage dedicated to the Sakhalin II project.
Organizations like the Society of Gas Tankers and Terminal Operators have been instrumental in highlighting the crewing issue. SIGTTO has developed a "training initiative" that sets minimum operational standards for all ten officer ranks on an LNG tanker. SIGTTO's "best practice" guidelines are respected throughout the industry, although there are concerns that some new players may not be committed to these principles. Several firms have offered very low charter rates to break into the business, and the cost pressures arising from this strategy may encourage them to cut corners on maintenance and crew training. As a result, many charterers now require that crews be trained to SIGTTO accredited standard. These guidelines are now being considered for adoption by the International Maritime Organization and may be included in a revision of the Standards of Training, Certification of Watch Keeping code.
A typical LNG vessel needs a complement of 27 seafarers comprising five deck officers, five engineer officers and 17 crew members. An additional complement is needed to account for vacations, illness and turnover. Retirements, illnesses and unplanned events can increase crewing needs even more. Shipping experts place the full officer requirement at three to three and a half times an operating complement and about two times for the crew, totaling 64 to 70 seafarers for each vessel. Based on the current order book, this would put incremental crewing needs at 8,500 to 9,200 mariners. It is presumed this total includes "poaching" of experienced seafarers for onshore jobs. Experienced officers are often in line for these attractive positions, draining much needed know-how from maritime operations.
Sourcing trained engineers presents a particularly thorny problem. There has been very little steam engineer training around the world during the last 50 years as the shipping sector has largely moved to diesel propulsion.

Legislation is afoot to require 2.4 million bbl/day of US ethanol use by 2022 - of which about one million bbl/day are mandated to come from corn-based production and the rest from "cellulosic" sources. While the process to turn corn into ethanol has been practiced for centuries, the process for teasing it from cellulosic sources is still merely a laboratory curiosity. The idea of leaving no tree behind in the quest for fuel ethanol might have a long road to travel before an economically viable commercial process is ever reached.
Legislation that bets on the scale-up of unproven technology to provide 1.4 million bbl/day of cellulosic-based ethanol to the nation's fuel supply within 15 years may create risks. To some, this bet is tantamount to betting that people would walk on the moon within a decade of the first successful flight of a liquid-fueled rocket in the mid- 1920's. It is one thing to push technology to new levels of performance as this legislation would. But it is quite another thing to pin consumers' hopes of ample fuel by 2022 from a still-to-be commercialized method.

Year-to-year changes in flat rates are intended to catch up with the cost fluctuations in various freight components of the previous year. Tanker owner spot market revenues are beholding to the agreed Worldscale rate for a given voyage. Consider a voyage Ras Tanura - Yokohama on 260k using 2007 average IFO and MDO costs: a movement from the present spot market of WS 280 to WS 290 using 2007 flat rate of $17.43/MT yields a differential of $441,850 on a lumpsum basis. Using 2008's flat rate of $18.25/MT increases this differential by nearly $21,000.
At a given Worldscale rate, any swing in bunker prices obviously goes right to an owner's bottom line. As an example, for the above voyage at a Worldscale of 280, the difference in revenue between 2007's high and low monthly bunker price equates to just over $460,000 or about ten Worldscale points. Not surprising then, bunker price volatility translates directly into revenue volatility.
